title: I Used the Company Christmas Party Seating to End the Joke

parts.text: I sat down at the company Christmas party nobody wanted and found my name card had been rewritten. I am twenty-seven, dental receptionist energy in a corporate admin job, notes on everything. The ballroom smelled like pine spray and meatballs. My coworker Grant had been doing a bit for months: I report everything, I can't take a joke, watch out. He thought it was bonding. I thought it was a file. I photographed the name card. My friend from billing, Naomi, whispered, "Don't give him the show." Grant clinked a glass. "Toast to the people who keep us legal." Eyes on me. I smiled the way I smile at late patients. The DJ played a song too loud for talk. Grant slid into the next chair. "Relax. It's comedy." I said, "Comedy doesn't require a Sharpie on a place card." He leaned closer, beer-warm. "If you walk that to HR, you prove the bit." That was the trap, and he said it out loud, which was generous. She said sure. "You two good?" Grant said, "We're great." I turned the name card around so Paul could read HR-BAIT. The pine spray suddenly smelled like a classroom. Then the DJ cut the music for speeches, and Grant stood up with a microphone he had not been given, and my work phone lit with a calendar invite he had just sent: Monday 1:1, let's clear the air before you do something stupid.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: He has the mic and a Monday invite that frames me as the problem if I report the Sharpie.

social.video_title: He Sharpie'd my place card HR-BAIT — Part 1/2
social.description: Pine spray, meatballs, and a toast that pointed. The vendor photographer had the frame. Would you have flipped the card for your director?

parts.text: I did not grab the mic. I forwarded the Monday invite to Paul and to HR with the photo of the card and Elise's table shot attached, timestamped. Then I sat down and ate a meatball, which was dry, which felt correct. Grant told a joke that died in the pine spray. After speeches, HR's on-call partner asked me to step into a hallway that still had coat racks. I gave them the file I had been keeping, because I do take notes. Grant said, "It was a bit." I said, "The invite said something stupid." The invite language, something stupid, did not land as comedy. He got a written warning and a seating chart that was not near mine. He told the team I couldn't take a joke. Naomi said, "The joke had a Sharpie." I updated my resume anyway. People confuse documentation with disloyalty. I am loyal to my nervous system. The recap blog never used the photo. Elise sent it to me anyway, and I keep it. At next year's party, which I skipped, they used printed names under plastic. Someone still tried a nickname. Paul shut it down. I work elsewhere now, still admin, still notes. Sometimes I smell pine spray in grocery aisles and laugh once. Grant LinkedIn-congratulated me on the new job. I archived it. The meatballs at the new place are also dry. That, I can live with. The Sharpie, I could not.

social.video_title: The Monday invite became the exhibit — Part 2/2
social.description: I ate the dry meatball and forwarded the 1:1 that told me not to do something stupid. Printed names went under plastic the next year. Would you have skipped the next party?
